fixes.explanation: No war in this order, friend. The LORD tells David, Israel's king, “Go and take a census of Israel and Judah.” That's the order the text gives, a count of Israel and Judah.
The ark isn't part of this order. The LORD tells David, Israel's king, “Go and take a census of Israel and Judah.” It's a count of the people, nothing about moving anything holy anywhere.

Homes aren't in David's words here. He tells Joab to register the troops “…so that I may know their number.” The goal he states is a total of the troops, not a map of where everybody lives. The missing word is number.

False is right, and Joab is the reason. Joab, the commander of David's army, says, “But why does my lord the king want to do such a thing?” (2 Samuel 24:3). He's the one in the meeting who asks whether we're sure about this. I think everybody needs a Joab around.

The king's word wins. The text says, “Nevertheless, the king’s word prevailed against Joab and against the commanders of the army.” (2 Samuel 24:4). Joab and the commanders push back, and it still doesn't change the order. Push all they like, the king's word carries the day.

The commanders pushed back right alongside Joab, friend, but they don't win it. The text says, “Nevertheless, the king’s word prevailed against Joab and against the commanders of the army.” (2 Samuel 24:4). That's a whole lot of army leadership leaning on one decision, and the king's word is still the one that stands. Then Joab and the commanders head out to register the troops.

True. After the count, “…his conscience was stricken…” and David says to the LORD, “I have sinned greatly in what I have done.” (2 Samuel 24:10). He says it to the LORD himself. Gad hasn't shown up yet at that point.

It's actually true, friend. After the count, “…his conscience was stricken…” and David says to the LORD, “I have sinned greatly in what I have done.” (2 Samuel 24:10). He says it to the LORD himself. So David doesn't stay quiet about it.

I'd love to hand you a well, friend, but the angel isn't standing at one. The text says the angel of the LORD was “…by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.” (2 Samuel 24:16). Araunah is a Jebusite, and that's the place to remember. Bethlehem isn't mentioned here.

A pool sounds like a nice cool spot for an angel, friend, but the text puts him somewhere else. It says the angel of the LORD was “…by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.” (2 Samuel 24:16). Araunah is a Jebusite. Gibeon isn't in this verse at all.

The commanders aren't in David's request. He says, “Please, let Your hand fall upon me and my father’s house.” (2 Samuel 24:17). He asks for it to fall on himself and his own family. The shepherd steps in front of the sheep.

An altar is right. Gad, David's prophet and seer, says, “Go up and build an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.” (2 Samuel 24:18). The instruction comes that same day, after David speaks to the LORD.

A house for the ark is a big project, friend, but it isn't the one Gad brings. He's David's prophet and seer, and he says, “Go up and build an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.” (2 Samuel 24:18). Altar first. That's the order, and that's the place.

The guard can stand down, friend, because no watchtower is in this order. Gad, David's prophet and seer, says, “Go up and build an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.” (2 Samuel 24:18). The word is altar, and the place is Araunah's threshing floor.

Not quite, friend. The text says, “So David went up at the word of Gad, just as the LORD had commanded.” (2 Samuel 24:19). David goes up himself. Araunah looks out and sees “…the king and his servants coming toward him…” (2 Samuel 24:20).

True. Araunah gives it all to the king, but David answers, “No… I insist on paying a price, for I will not offer to the LORD my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing.” (2 Samuel 24:24). Then he buys the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.
